span: the circumstantial evidence in order to sustain conviction must be complete and incapable of explanation of any other hypothesis than that of guilt of the accused
why: Court says the law on circumstantial evidence 'was aptly dealt with' in Padala Veera Reddy and uses those tests: conviction can be sustained when they are met.

span: to convict an accused on the basis of circumstantial evidence, the Court must follow certain tests which are broadly as follows
why: Court sets out the tests for convicting on circumstantial evidence and in the next paragraph says an accused can be punished on it if the complete chain is proved.

span: In order to sustain a conviction, it is imperative that the chain of circumstances is complete, cogent and coherent.
why: Headnote states the condition for sustaining a conviction on circumstantial evidence and finds it unmet for the main accused.

span: an accused can be punished if he is found guilty even in cases of circumstantial evidence provided, the prosecution is able to prove beyond reasonable doubt the complete chain of events and circumstances
why: Headnote holding: no eyewitness is not a ground for acquittal; conviction on circumstantial evidence is permissible on proof of the complete chain.

span: every circumstance must be fully proved and all the circumstances must form a chain of evidence so complete as to exclude every hypothesis other than the guilt of the accused
why: Headnote states the standard and holds it unmet on the facts, resulting in acquittal.
